blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Class-incremental learning (CIL) for outdoor 3D object detection remains largely underexplored. Existing outdoor studies are limited to single-benchmark evaluations, with SDCoT++ considering KITTI and CL2OD considering nuScenes under different incremental settings. This makes it difficult to assess whether observed continual-learning behavior generalizes across autonomous-driving benchmarks. To the best of our knowledge, we provide the first unified cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object detection across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks, covering both two-task and multi-stage settings. We investigate: (1) how severely existing 3D detectors forget previously learned classes, (2) how incremental training exposes the stability-plasticity dilemma between knowledge retention and new-class acquisition, and (3) which forms of supervision are most effective for balancing these objectives. We introduce CL3DOD, a class-incremental 3D detection framework that restores missing supervision for previous classes using predictions from the previous-stage detector, preserves old-class responses through query-wise knowledge distillation, and employs EMA-based temporal consistency regularization. Experiments on KITTI and nuScenes reveal a consistent stability-plasticity dilemma across both benchmarks. CL3DOD generally achieves a more favorable stability-plasticity balance than controlled incremental baselines and improves upon published prior methods in the reported benchmark comparisons. This advantage persists across multiple incremental stages, demonstrating strong retention of previously learned knowledge while maintaining effective new-class acquisition. Our code, evaluation setup, and incremental task splits will be publicly released.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Autonomous vehicles may need to recognize object categories that were
absent or insufficiently annotated during initial training. Retraining a
3D detector whenever new classes are introduced can require access to
large amounts of previously annotated data, making continual updates
costly and impractical. Class-incremental learning (CIL) addresses this
problem by enabling sequential acquisition of new categories while
preserving previously learned knowledge [ 13 , 20 ] . This is particularly
relevant to LiDAR-based 3D object detection, a core component of
autonomous-driving perception [ 8 , 2 ] .

blocks.en:
The challenge, however, is not catastrophic forgetting alone.
Incremental learning must balance the retention of previous knowledge
( stability ) with the ability to acquire new knowledge
( plasticity ). This stability-plasticity dilemma [ 11 ] is further complicated in object detection
because old and current classes can co-occur in the same scene while
only current-class annotations are available, causing unlabeled old
objects to be treated as background. Existing class-incremental 3D
detection methods address this problem through pseudo-labeling,
distillation, parameter isolation, and teacher-student consistency [ 25 , 27 , 6 , 26 ] .
Their evaluation, however, has largely emphasized knowledge retention
and aggregate detection performance, with plasticity less commonly
quantified explicitly.

blocks.en:
Class-incremental 3D detection in outdoor autonomous-driving scenes
remains particularly underexplored. Most existing studies focus on
indoor settings [ 25 , 27 , 6 , 26 ] ,
while the available outdoor evaluations are limited to individual
benchmarks: SDCoT++ [ 26 ] reports results on KITTI,
whereas CL2OD [ 22 ] studies nuScenes under a different
incremental formulation. Consequently, it remains unclear whether the
same stability-plasticity behavior and continual-learning mechanisms
generalize across different outdoor autonomous-driving benchmarks. To
the best of our knowledge, no prior work provides a unified
cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object
detection across multiple autonomous-driving datasets. We therefore ask
three questions: (1) How severe is forgetting in outdoor 3D detection? (2) How does incremental learning affect the stability-plasticity balance ? (3) Which supervision signals are effective for preserving
old knowledge while learning new classes?

blocks.en:
Class-incremental learning (CIL) aims to acquire new categories
sequentially while retaining previously learned knowledge. Existing
approaches primarily rely on regularization [ 12 , 23 , 1 ] , knowledge distillation [ 13 , 10 , 7 ] , and
rehearsal [ 15 , 4 ] to mitigate catastrophic forgetting [ 16 ] .
However, retention alone does not fully characterize continual learning:
a model must remain stable on previous knowledge while preserving
sufficient plasticity to acquire new concepts. Chaudhry et al. [ 3 ] formalize this distinction through
forgetting and intransigence, while Kim and Han [ 11 ] further show that modern CIL methods can favor
stability at the expense of plasticity.

依次保留以前学到的知识。 现有
方法主要依赖正规化[12、23、1]、知识蒸馏[13、10、7]和
排练 [15,4] 减轻灾难性遗忘 [16].
然而,仅保留一个人并不能充分说明持续学习的特点:
模式必须保持以往知识的稳定,同时保持

忘记和不妥协, 而金和汉 [11] 进一步表明,现代 CIL 方法可以赞成
稳定性以可塑性为代价。

blocks.en:
CIL has also been extended to object detection, where previously learned
objects may appear without annotations during later tasks and consequently
be treated as background. Shmelkov et al. [ 20 ] introduce knowledge distillation for
incremental 2D detection, while subsequent methods explore feature- and
output-level distillation [ 5 , 9 ] and
pseudo-label-based supervision [ 14 ] . The broader
continual object detection literature similarly emphasizes the need to
consider both retention and adaptation when evaluating incremental
detectors [ 17 ] .

More recently, CIL has been studied for point-cloud-based 3D object
detection. SDCoT [ 25 ] introduces a teacher-student
framework using pseudo-label recovery, distillation, and consistency,
while SDCoT++ [ 26 ] improves pseudo-label generation
and evaluates the framework across different 3D detectors. DA-CIL [ 27 ] considers class-incremental detection under domain
shift, and AIC3DOD [ 6 ] studies indoor incremental
detection with a point-transformer architecture and room-layout
constraints. Recent work also investigates longer incremental sequences
in indoor 3D detection [ 19 ] . In outdoor scenes,
SDCoT++ reports results on KITTI, while CL2OD [ 22 ] studies nuScenes under a different incremental
formulation. Despite this progress, systematic analysis across multiple
outdoor autonomous-driving benchmarks remains limited, particularly with
respect to the stability-plasticity behavior across both short and
multi-stage incremental settings.

blocks.en:
Inspired by teacher-student strategies for class-incremental 3D
detection [ 25 , 6 ] , we introduce CL3DOD , a class-incremental framework for outdoor 3D object
detection. We use Uni3DETR [ 21 ] as the underlying
3D detector due to its strong outdoor LiDAR-only detection performance
and modern DETR-style formulation, making it a representative
architecture for studying class-incremental learning in outdoor scenes.
The detector is first trained conventionally on 𝒯 1 \mathcal{T}_{1} ,
yielding the initial model f θ 1 f_{\theta_{1}} . For each subsequent task 𝒯 t \mathcal{T}_{t} , the detector f θ t − 1 f_{\theta_{t-1}} from the preceding
stage initializes the current student , while a frozen copy
serves as the previous-stage teacher carrying knowledge of 𝒞 1 : t − 1 \mathcal{C}_{1:t-1} . An EMA teacher is additionally
initialized from the student and updated as an exponential moving
average of its parameters. The overall framework is illustrated in
Fig. 1 .

blocks.en: 4.1 Experimental Setup
blocks.zh: 4.1 实验设置

blocks.en:
We evaluate CL3DOD on two outdoor autonomous-driving benchmarks,
KITTI [ 8 ] and nuScenes [ 2 ] .
KITTI contains relatively few sufficiently populated categories and is
therefore evaluated using a two-task class-incremental split. The split
consists of 𝒯 1 \mathcal{T}_{1} : Car, Pedestrian, and Cyclist; and 𝒯 2 \mathcal{T}_{2} : Van and Truck. The first task corresponds to the
standard categories commonly used for KITTI 3D detection evaluation,
while the second introduces driving-relevant but less frequent
categories, thereby retaining the naturally long-tailed class
distribution of the dataset. This partition is also consistent with the
KITTI setting used by SDCoT and SDCoT++, enabling comparison with
existing class-incremental 3D detection results.

blocks.en:
nuScenes provides a richer taxonomy of ten official detection classes,
allowing us to evaluate a more challenging three-task class-incremental
setting. The split consists of 𝒯 1 \mathcal{T}_{1} : Car, Trailer, and
Construction Vehicle; 𝒯 2 \mathcal{T}_{2} : Bus, Truck, and Pedestrian; and 𝒯 3 \mathcal{T}_{3} : Motorcycle, Bicycle, Traffic Cone, and Barrier.
This partition preserves the heterogeneous and long-tailed nature of
nuScenes: 𝒯 1 \mathcal{T}_{1} combines a dominant vehicle category with
rarer vehicle classes, 𝒯 2 \mathcal{T}_{2} contains dynamic traffic

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
In this work, we provide, to the best of our knowledge, the first
unified cross-benchmark analysis of outdoor class-incremental 3D object
detection across multiple autonomous-driving benchmarks. Experiments on
KITTI and nuScenes reveal a clear stability-plasticity dilemma,
highlighting the need to evaluate both knowledge retention and new-class
acquisition.

We introduce CL3DOD , combining Old-Class Supervision,

including across the multi-stage nuScenes setting. Our ablations

mechanism, while the effects of distillation and temporal consistency
vary across datasets. Future work can explore longer incremental
sequences and more selective knowledge-transfer and replay strategies.

blocks.en:
We build CL3DOD on the outdoor Uni3DETR [ 21 ] configurations. Uni3DETR employs a hybrid
sparse-dense 3D feature extractor followed by a DETR-style decoder
operating on learnable and non-learnable queries. For class-incremental training, we extend the classification output to
the cumulative class set and maintain a frozen previous-stage teacher
and an EMA teacher.
We additionally expose the FPS-derived non-learnable query points and
reuse the same queries for the student and previous-stage teacher,
enabling the query-aligned distillation described in the main paper.
The underlying feature extractor and Transformer decoder otherwise
remain unchanged.

blocks.en: 10.1 Failure Cases
blocks.zh: 10.1 失败案件

blocks.en:
Figure 5 presents representative failure cases
of CL3DOD after incremental learning on Task 2. Although CL3DOD
substantially mitigates catastrophic forgetting, it does not completely
preserve all previously learned objects. In some scenes, the model
correctly detects several objects while missing others that are present
in the ground-truth annotations. These failures are particularly visible
for distant or sparsely represented objects, where limited LiDAR
observations make localization and classification more challenging.
We also observe cases in which only a subset of the annotated objects
is recovered, indicating that retention of previous knowledge remains
imperfect after the incremental update.

These examples highlight a remaining limitation of CL3DOD: preserving
old-class knowledge at the model level does not guarantee successful
detection of every old-class instance under challenging scene
conditions. Improving instance-level retention, particularly for sparse
and difficult objects, therefore remains an important direction for
future class-incremental 3D detection.
